title: Symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity
authors: Cunshen Li, Rong Li, Jiongning Che, Cheng-Zhen Wang, Liang Huang
abstract: Nonreciprocity enriches wave control and information processing through directional transport, yet challenges conventional in-situ physical adjoint optimization, which relies on reciprocity to acquire adjoint responses. Here we demonstrate symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing (Sym-iPAC) in nonreciprocal systems, which enables access to adjoint responses on the original hardware through three classes of transpose symmetry: local geometric permutations, complex gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry in effective port dynamics revealed by Schur reduction. Experiments with programmable nonreciprocal microwave networks validate these transpose relations and yield adjoint gradients, enabling closed-loop optimization. These results establish experimentally accessible transpose symmetry as a route to in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity.
summary: This work presents a novel method, Sym-iPAC, to perform adjoint gradient calculations in nonreciprocal wave systems, overcoming the limitation that conventional adjoint methods require system reciprocity. By exploiting three types of structured transpose symmetries—geometric permutation, gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry—the authors enable closed-loop optimization directly on the original hardware using microwave networks. This establishes a general, experimentally accessible route for advanced wave control beyond reciprocal regimes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of performing in-situ physical adjoint computing for wave control in nonreciprocal systems, where standard adjoint methods fail due to the lack of reciprocity.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrate Symmetry-driven in-situ Physical Adjoint Computing (Sym-iPAC) using three classes of experimentally accessible transpose symmetries, enabling closed-loop optimization.
method: They utilize structured transpose mappings (Permutation, Gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry from Schur reduction) to calculate adjoint gradients directly on the original nonreciprocal hardware.
model_or_system: The experiments are conducted using programmable nonreciprocal microwave networks, which are modeled by scattering matrices (S-matrices) that are generally non-symmetric.
key_observables: Scattering matrix (S), adjoint gradients (d{g}/d{p}), and the objective function's evolution during closed-loop optimization.
important_parameters: The three symmetry types (Permutation, Gauge, Latent) and the tunable parameters of the microwave components (e.g., $\Delta L_{78}$).
main_assumptions: The mapping D must be fixed throughout parameter tuning, and the method relies on finding experimentally accessible transpose symmetries.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between reciprocal and nonreciprocal systems, and show optimization trajectories and gradient comparisons across the three symmetry types (Permutation, Gauge, Latent).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of nonreciprocal adjoint computing, details the three symmetry-driven solutions (Permutation, Gauge, Latent), validates these symmetries using measured residuals, and finally demonstrates closed-loop optimization by comparing adjoint gradients against finite-difference methods.
why_interesting: While focused on microwave circuits, the core concept of using structured symmetries to bypass physical constraints (like reciprocity) to enable gradient computation is highly relevant to optimizing complex quantum control protocols in open quantum systems.
